newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Deng concerns shake China, Taiwan, HK stocks.
newsitem.headline: Deng concerns shake China, Taiwan, HK stocks.

text.p: Concerns over the health of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping rocked Chinese, Taiwan and Hong Kong stock markets on Tuesday, with Shenzhen taking the biggest hit by the close, brokers said.

Investor attention turned to Beijing after sources said on Monday that Deng's deteriorating health had forced Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin and other leaders to cut short provincial trips to return to the capital.
China's Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday there had been no major change in the health of 92-year-old Deng.

"We have had these rumours about Deng Xiaoping passing into the great unknown every three weeks for the last three years but this one seems to have a little more substance to it," said Peter Churchouse, regional strategist at Morgan Stanley.
"When Deng departs there will inevitably be a degree of uncertainty and stock markets don't like uncertainty," he said.
Analysts said worries were likely to linger in the short term and investors should expect more volatility.
"There is some confusion over what his state of health is. Things look a little rough through this week," said Andrew Fernow, director of research at Vickers Ballas.
Particularly worrying, he said, was that talk of Deng's health had been affecting trading over the past few sessions. "People are more nervous than they have been in the past," he said.
In the currency market, worries about Deng's health gave psychological support to the dollar, which rose as high as 124.70 yen.
"At this point, it would be a momentary positive for the dollar," said Kenneth Landon, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Tokyo.
He said this would be particularly true against the yen, which would be most at risk because of Japan's geographical proximity to China. "But I wouldn't expect any major political changes," he added.
The Hong Kong dollar weakened slightly against the U.S. dollar, testing the 7.75 level from Monday's 7.7497, but traders said activity was light.

Among the China-related stock markets, share prices in Shenzhen were hit hardest. The B-share index plummeted 14.59 points, or 9.58 percent, to close at 137.72 while the A-share index ended down 36.53 points, or 9.76 percent, at 337.65.
In Shanghai, the B-share index lost 4.754 points, or 6.97 percent, to 63.455 and the A-share index fell 91.94 points, or 8.97 percent, to 932.783.
"The China market tends to provide a barometer on the political sentiment," said Fernow.

In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng Index managed to crawl back from its lows to end only modestly weaker. The blue-chip index ended off 41.68 points, or 0.32 percent, at 13,102.94 after tumbling to a morning low of 12,933.98 points.
In Taiwan, the weighted index ended down 45.15 points, or 0.59 percent, to 7,642.03.

Analysts in Taiwan said the Deng rumours had a psychological impact but added the drop was mainly in response to comments late on Monday by central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong, who said the bullish bourse had risen "slightly too much" in recent days.
The slump came at a time of across-the-board weakness in Asian stock markets. Strategists said while bourses were experiencing a knee-jerk reaction, the Deng issue should not have a lingering impact.

"The key issue is that he has not held political office for a considerable period of time and his influence is more as a patriarchal figure," said Abhijit Chakrabortti, senior strategist at Lehman Brothers.
